title: King Ladder??
summary: Walk the king down the bishops’ diagonals, releasing the pinned knight just long enough to avoid stalemate.

nodes.question: How can White improve without allowing promotion?
nodes.explanation: The bishops control a2 and c1, while Black’s own knight and pawns restrict its king. White must preserve useful legal moves for Black.

nodes.question: Why does a random king move draw immediately?
nodes.explanation: With the pawn now on a3, Black’s king and pawns are immobilized and the b2 knight is pinned to Ka1. White must interrupt a bishop diagonal before Black can move.

nodes.question: What changes once the white king reaches c2?
nodes.explanation: The king can now help the bishops remove a3 and set up mate. Capturing Nb2 too early would replace the pinned knight with a dangerous passed pawn after ...axb2.

branches.title: Release the knight and walk down the board
commentary: Begin from the complete seven-piece diagram. Follow one selected illustrated route through the knight’s defenses; not all legal replies are enumerated.
Bg6+ checks along g6–b1 and controls b1, tightening the black king’s cage.
Ka1 retreats into the corner, where Black’s own a2 pawn limits its king.
Kf7 approaches the bishop diagonals so the king can later interrupt them deliberately.
Nd1 attacks Be3, inviting White to find a useful checking bishop retreat.
Bd4+ saves the bishop with check along d4–a1.
Nb2 blocks the check and returns to the square pinning the knight to its king.
Bg7 restores the long diagonal and prepares the king’s controlled interference.
a3 uses Black’s remaining pawn move. Now the pawns block one another, creating the stalemate danger.
Kf6 blocks Bg7’s diagonal, unpinning the knight rather than leaving Black without a legal move.
Nd3 uses that released diagonal to move the knight. It now blocks the g6 bishop’s line to b1.
Ke6+ reopens Bg7’s diagonal and checks the cornered king.
Nb2 blocks the discovered check and restores the original pin.
Ke5 interrupts Bg7’s diagonal again, allowing the knight another move.
Nd3+ uses the release and checks the white king on e5.
Kd5+ escapes the knight check while reopening the bishop’s check on Ka1.
Nb2 interposes once more, keeping Black alive.
Kd4 interrupts Bg7’s diagonal on the next lower square and unpins the knight.
Na4 is the illustrated knight move; it occupies the a-file above Black’s pawns.
Kc4+ steps off the bishop line, giving another discovered check.
Nb2+ blocks that check and checks Kc4 with the knight.
Kc3 answers the knight check while deliberately blocking the bishop diagonal.
Na4+ leaves the unpinned square and checks White again.
Kc2+ answers the check and reveals Bg7’s diagonal toward Ka1.
Nb2 is again required in this selected route to cover the discovered check.
Bf8 changes the bishop’s diagonal and prepares to capture a3 with support from the approaching king.
Nc4 guards a3, trying to prevent its capture.
Kb3 approaches the pawn and attacks Nc4, making the guard unstable.
Nb2 returns to the corner defense but no longer protects a3.
Bxa3 removes that pawn. With the white king close, the mating construction is now possible.
Nc4 keeps the knight active and controls b2, the intended mating square.
Bc1 waits while preserving control of b2. Black cannot leave its knight on c4 forever.
Nb2 is the source’s final illustrated knight return. It moves onto the square where White can capture with mate.
Bxb2# is the independently completed actual mate: Kb3 protects the bishop, Bg6 controls b1 and the a2 pawn blocks Black’s other flight.

branches.title: Leave the cage completely closed
commentary: Compare a legal independent king move that does not interrupt either bishop’s diagonal.
Ke8 is actual stalemate. Ka1 is not in check, Nb2 cannot leave the diagonal pin, the pawns are blocked and the king has no legal flight.
branches.classification: independent alternative with representative legal replies
branches.explanation: Ke8 is actual stalemate. Ka1 is not in check, Nb2 cannot leave the diagonal pin, the pawns are blocked and the king has no legal flight.

branches.title: The knight chooses the a-file
commentary: Compare the source’s alternative knight move after the bishop switch.
Bf8 prepares the capture on a3 without allowing that pawn to promote.
Na4 leaves a3 undefended and abandons the c4 control of b2.
Bxa3 removes the pawn and threatens Bb2 mate.
Nb2 is an independently selected representative return; Black cannot use the knight as a permanent guard of b2 from a4.
Bxb2# captures the knight and is actual mate. The bishop is protected by Kc2, while Bg6 closes b1 and a2 is occupied by Black’s pawn.
branches.classification: selected source alternative with independent representative knight reply and mating completion
branches.explanation: Bb2# is actual mate. The bishop is protected by Kc2 and blocks the knight’s route, while Bg6 closes b1.

exercises.prompt: Why must White temporarily weaken its bishop control?
exercises.answer: Black otherwise has no legal move. The king blocks a bishop diagonal to release the pinned knight, then steps off that diagonal to check and force it back.
Bxb2 lets ...axb2 replace the pinned knight with a passed pawn protected by Ka1. Bf8 first reorganizes the bishops so a3 can be removed safely.

startContext: The complete seven-piece board and selected long king-ladder route are reconstructed from saved images. The final Bxb2 mating completions are independently supplied and labeled; the source ends its main illustration after ...Nb2. The random-move stalemate comparison is independent.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
